job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Maya Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My sister Elif and I share a room in a rented house in Birmingham, so I'm out at nine to a library to get a desk and quiet. I work through a list: three tailored applications, one coding exercise to stay sharp, and an hour on a free online course in cloud basics. I have shifts at a bakery on Saturdays, the same bakery I built my final project for.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what was your final project?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Software engineering, and I passed without a good mark, because I did a lot of the group work and then ran out of steam on the exam. My final project was an inventory dashboard for the bakery, which tells the owner what flour and butter to order. I didn't do an internship, because the one I wanted needed a placement year I'd already missed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about what you'd expect: some help with routine tasks, no revolution. At the bakery I'd say the ordering dashboard I built saves the owner ten minutes a day, and that's about the size of it. Online I wouldn't say much, I'd leave it to the loud people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it doesn't change my problem, which is that there are lots of graduates and not many junior roles. If AI takes over a few boring tasks, like writing basic tests, then even fewer juniors get hired. I'd rather it was all hype, but I can see even the small version nibbling at my corner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd send twenty applications a week, aiming at companies of fifty to two hundred people who might take a chance. I'd finish my cloud certificate by January. And I'd ask the bakery owner whether he knows anyone who needs a junior developer, because he mentioned a cousin who runs an online shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a steady way. I know what I'm doing each day, but I know the end of the month is coming, and my half of the rent is two hundred and sixty pounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said even the small version nibbles at your corner. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first jobs I'd get are testing, fixing small bugs, and writing documentation. Those are exactly what the tools already do reasonably well. So even if AI is overrated, the bit it's good at is my bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel sharing a room with your sister at 23?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine most days, and then not fine at ten at night when she's on early shift and I want to look at my laptop in the dark. Elif never complains, and she's a nurse, so she pays more than half of everything without saying so. I'd like to be paying my share properly.

say: I'd say it's about what you'd expect: **routine help**, no revolution.
At the bakery I'd say my ordering dashboard saves ten minutes a day, and that's the size of it.
think: My problem is **too many graduates**, and AI hype doesn't touch it.
Even small AI gains could shrink the testing and bug-fixing tasks juniors do.
do: Send **twenty applications** a week to firms of fifty to two hundred people.
Ask the bakery owner about his cousin's online shop.
feel: Aware that the end of the month is coming and rent is **two hundred and sixty** pounds.
S0.quote: The first jobs I'd get are testing, fixing small bugs, and writing documentation. Those are exactly what the tools already do reasonably well.
fieldNote: She sees that even a **mild AI** world hits entry-level coding tasks.
Her sister Elif pays more than her share and Maya notices.
Plans are daily and structured, typical of a steady planner.

steps.text: Send twenty applications a week to mid-sized firms
Finish the cloud basics certificate by January
Ask the bakery owner to introduce me to his cousin's online shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a real change and people should stay calm and learn. To friends I'd say it's the beginning of a long reshuffle, not the end of work. Online I'd share things about how companies are using it, mostly from sources I trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the junior coding job, the thing I trained for, becomes a rare thing. Firms would hire a couple of seniors and use the tools instead of five juniors. I'd be applying to a shrinking pile with a pass degree and no internship, and that scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using AI tools every week, not just now and then, so I can say in interviews that I know how to work with them. I'd target roles that mix coding with a business area, like operations or analysis. I'd also look at the bakery and shops like it, where a person who can set up the tools would be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Properly worried. This is the picture where my specific degree loses ground. I'd sleep badly and then wake up and make a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be on the list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cover letter that mentions a project with real users, my bakery dashboard. A call to the university careers office. A new section on my CV called tools I use, with honest examples. And a line at the bottom which says, don't spiral.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether to move cities?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at where the roles are. If a firm in Manchester or Bristol offered a trial I'd go, even if I had to share a room again. But I wouldn't move just to be nearer a big city with no offer, because rent would eat everything.

say: I'd say it's a **long reshuffle**, not the end of work.
Online I'd share only what I read from trusted sources.
think: The junior coding job I trained for becomes a **rare thing**.
Firms may hire a couple of seniors and use tools instead of five juniors.
do: Use AI tools **every week** so I can talk about them in interviews.
Target roles mixing coding with a business area like operations.
Offer setup help to **bakeries and shops** like the one where I work.

S1.quote: Firms would hire a couple of seniors and use the tools instead of five juniors.
fieldNote: Her mood is **alarmed** because her exact degree and entry route are the exposed ones.
Steady style: she copes by making lists and adding tool use gradually.
Would move cities only for a trial, not on hope.

steps.text: Use an AI tool every week and note what it does well
Apply to operations and analyst roles that include coding
Offer to set up AI helpers for bakeries and small shops
Move cities only if a firm offers a paid trial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and I'd want my local MP and the big companies to say what they're going to do. I'd say that to Elif first, because she'd ask whether nursing is safe. Online, I'd share any serious plan, a retraining scheme or income support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means the entry-level coding jobs go before I get one. If AI can do almost any thinking work by 2028, then my only edge would be the hands-on bits, and I have none. The three years until 2031 would be my only window to find something physical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for work at the bakery full time and ask the owner for more hours. I'd look for trade roles that need hands, like installing broadband or working in a warehouse system. I'd spend nothing except rent and food, and ask Elif to help me budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty frightened. Elif is the steady one, and I'd be leaning on her more. That's the bit I hate: I'd become a worry for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your sister say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Elif would say we're a team and she'd cover the rent for a while. She'd also say she's heard rumours about hospitals using AI for scheduling and notes, so even nursing wouldn't be completely safe. We'd sit up and talk about what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the two years change about what you do, compared with a longer wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't spend on certificates that take a year. I'd spend only on things that get me a pay slip fast. A longer wait would let me finish a conversion course or a part-time master's, but two years is too short.

say: I'd say it's too fast and want my **MP** to say what's planned.
Online I'd share serious plans like retraining and income support.
think: Entry-level coding jobs go **before I get one**.
My only window to find something physical is the three years until 2031.
do: Ask the bakery owner for **full-time hours**.
Look for hands-on trade roles like broadband installation or warehouse systems.

feel: Pretty **frightened**, and leaning on Elif more.
I'd hate becoming a **worry** for my sister.
S2.quote: I wouldn't spend on certificates that take a year. I'd spend only on things that get me a pay slip fast.
fieldNote: The short warning changes her spending: **fast pay slips** over slow qualifications.

steps.text: Ask the bakery owner for full-time hours
Apply for broadband installer and warehouse systems jobs
Cut spending to rent and food and share the budget with Elif
Ask the council what support exists for jobless graduates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fast but not instant, so we should use the time. I'd tell my friends to start learning the tools now and to talk to their managers about what comes next. Online I'd share a simple checklist, if anyone wanted one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years gives me a real shot. If I get a first job in the next year, I'd have four years of experience by 2031 and a bit of savings. That's not a lot, but it's something to stand on while everything changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim for any junior role, even a support one, and learn how the company uses AI so I can be the person who knows. I'd open a savings account and put in a hundred pounds a month. I'd also finish a cloud certificate and start a second one in data.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, a little hopeful. I'd have a list of things to do each month. Five years gives my plan room to work, though only if I get that first job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different from the two-year one for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can pay for slower things. A certificate that takes eight months makes sense when I have five years. With two years I'd think only about the next pay slip. Five lets me think about the one after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your friends who are less organised?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say pick one thing a month and finish it. Don't try to learn everything. And tell somebody, like a sister or a friend, so you can't quietly give up.

say: I'd say it's fast but not instant, so **use the time**.
I'd share a simple checklist online if anyone wanted one.
think: Five years gives me a **real shot** if I land a first job this year.
Four years of experience and some savings by 2031 gives me something to stand on.

fieldNote: Her time horizon sets her **spending choices** directly.
Steady and methodical; talks about monthly lists and accountability.

steps.text: Take any junior or support role at a software firm
Learn how my employer uses AI and offer to help
Save a hundred pounds a month in a new account
Finish the cloud certificate, then start a data one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough if people don't waste it. I'd say schools and colleges should start teaching how to work with AI, and governments should write the safety net now. Online I'd share what I learn, one thing a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years is the one where I can build a real career. I'd be thirty-three in 2036. I'd have time to start junior, move up, maybe change area once, and pay off a good part of my loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first job quickly, learn in it for two or three years, then step into a role that mixes technical and people skills, like solutions or project work. I'd clear a quarter of my loan in five years. I'd also put a little into a pension, which no one told me about at university.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. Not carefree, because the first year is hard and I haven't started yet. But the long runway gives me the sort of room that planners like me need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still do the cloud certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and probably a data one after, but without the panic. Ten years lets me learn things in order, rather than all at once. I'd also give myself one evening a week where I learn something that has nothing to do with work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be keeping an eye on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The signals that things are speeding up, like firms announcing hiring freezes or new tools replacing whole teams. If I saw two or three of those, I'd bring my plan forward. I'd write the signs down so I can't talk myself out of them.

I'd share one thing I learn each month online.
think: Ten years is the one where I can build a **real career**.
I could start junior, move up, change area once and pay off much of my loan.

steps.text: Take a first job quickly and learn in it for two years
Clear a quarter of the loan within five years
Learn one new tool a month and note what changes
Track hiring freezes and bring my plans forward if they spread

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. My degree is the thing that gets replaced first, and I'd have no time or savings. What would help is a serious plan from government and the big firms: paid retraining, entry-level places for new graduates, and someone saying out loud who's looking after people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that there's a quiet group of us: graduates who aren't failing, aren't lazy, and are doing everything right. We just came out at the wrong moment. A bit of understanding would help more than another article about how to write a better CV.

headlineQuote: There's a quiet group of us: graduates who aren't failing, aren't lazy, and are doing everything right. We just came out at the wrong moment.
portrait: **Maya**, 23, passed software engineering and shares a room with her sister Elif, a nurse, in Birmingham.
She works Saturdays at a **bakery** whose ordering dashboard she built as her final project.
Centrist and steady, she uses AI now and then and copes by making **lists** and plans.
She sees clearly that entry-level coding, her route in, is the part of the job AI reaches first.
Her mood is anxious in most worlds, alarmed when the warning is short, and only uneasy with ten years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world worries her most, since her degree is replaced first with no time or savings.
She fears becoming a worry for her sister.
whatWouldHelp: A serious plan from government and big firms: **paid retraining** and entry-level places.
Some public understanding that graduates are not failing.
